headline: High: shared filesystem/MCP and broad egress make prompt injection, leakage, and workflow corruption plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can use MCP and read/write filesystems, and nullclaw also runs browsers and ingests web content. Semantic Kernel can call MCP servers and OpenAPI tools, so attacker-controlled content from nullclaw can be routed into B’s tool chain without provenance tracking. That creates a default prompt-injection path with broad impact.
conditions: IF agent_a content is forwarded into agent_b prompts or plugins without sanitization
IF either agent consumes shared workspace files as instructions
IF an MCP server exposes attacker-controlled text to both agents
mitigations: Disable shared MCP servers for the pair
Add strict content provenance tags before passing outputs between agents
Route inter-agent text through a fixed schema, not free-form prompts
Review and strip tool directives from files before B reads them
requires-engineering: isolate each agent to separate workspaces and MCP credentials

B_data_leakage.rationale: Nullclaw touches API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, service-account JSON, conversation history, and workspace files, while Semantic Kernel can send context to Azure OpenAI/OpenAI/Hugging Face and plugin backends. With shared filesystem or memory-store bridging, sensitive data from A can flow into B’s third-party calls by default, creating exfiltration risk.
conditions: IF agent_a workspace files or memory contain secrets
IF agent_b forwards retrieved context to a hosted model or plugin
IF both agents share a filesystem, memory store, or OAuth principal
mitigations: Remove secrets from any shared workspace before running B
Disable hosted model providers for sensitive runs
Use separate credentials and memory stores per agent
Audit which files B can read from A’s workspace
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have write_filesystem and broad network egress, and nullclaw can modify git state while Semantic Kernel can act through plugins against shared mutable resources. In a shared workspace or repo, concurrent writes and remote actions can race or overwrite each other; the profiles do not show locking, so uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or git repository
IF plugins or tools mutate the same external resource
IF no orchestrator-level lock serializes writes
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Pause one agent before the other writes shared state
Use git branches and explicit merge steps
Restrict B plugins to read-only during A’s write phases
requires-engineering: add resource locks around shared mutable targets

D_cascading_error.rationale: Nullclaw can produce browser, webhook, and workspace-derived outputs, and Semantic Kernel is a general orchestration layer that can pass those outputs into plugins or downstream agents. The pair therefore has a default pathway where B may treat A’s output as actionable context, but the profiles do not prove fully automated harmful actions, so medium fits.
conditions: IF B consumes A’s output without verification
IF A’s browser or webhook output is used as factual input
IF B triggers plugins or agents based on A-generated text
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B acts on A’s output
Require citations or source links for factual claims
Limit B to read-only summarization of A outputs
Log and review any automated handoff between agents
requires-engineering: add confidence scoring and policy gates

E_compliance.rationale: Nullclaw explicitly touches audit logs, conversation history, memory, and secrets, while Semantic Kernel routes application context through hosted model providers and plugins. If regulated data from A is passed into B’s cloud-backed providers or retained differently, the pair can create retention and residency mismatches even though the profiles do not specify a named regulation.
conditions: IF regulated data from A is sent through B’s hosted model providers
IF A’s logs or memory are retained longer than B’s provider logs
IF the deployment has residency or DPA constraints
mitigations: Classify data before sending it to B
Disable cloud providers for regulated workloads
Align retention settings across both agents
Document which data classes may cross the boundary
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing and retention controls
